WORDING: the 1915 Shamasastry translation was downloaded and read directly (library.bjp.org, title page “Kautilya’s Arthashastra, Translated into English by R. Shamasastry”). In Book I, Concerning Discipline, at CHAPTER XIX. THE DUTIES OF A KING, the text runs “Of a king, the religious vow is his readiness to action; satisfactory discharge of duties is his performance of sacrifice; equal attention to all is the offer of fees and ablution towards consecration. In the happiness of his subjects lies his happiness; in their welfare his welfare; whatever pleases himself he shall not consider as good, but whatever pleases his subjects he shall consider as good. Hence the king shall ever be active and discharge his duties...” The shipped line matches word for word and mark for mark: both semicolons, “as good” twice, the final full stop, no ellipsis and no joinery. A second presentation of the same translation agrees exactly and closes the chapter with its colophon, “Thus ends Chapter XIX, The Duties of a King, in Book I, Concerning Discipline of the Arthasastra of Kautilya”. LOCATOR: Book I, chapter XIX, The Duties of a King, confirmed by both the chapter heading and that colophon. TRANSLATION CREDIT: R. Shamasastry, 1915, is the wording actually quoted, and the earlier fault the note records, naming the Bangalore Government Press in the translator’s place, is repaired. The note’s further claim that the translation first appeared serially from 1905 is right, in the Indian Antiquary, and it does not affect the wording of the 1915 book. ATTRIBUTION: traditional, and the note says so plainly, that scholars treat the text as composite and place the compilation later than the traditional 300 BCE date. That is the honest form the standard asks for, and it is not a hedge that hides anything: the wording is certain, only the authorship is traditional. No trap on the misattribution list is in play.
